name: Preservation rhinoplasty

card.summary: Nose surgery that lowers or reshapes the bridge while keeping the natural dorsal structure intact rather than cutting a hump off; popular among surgeons, with mostly case-series evidence.
card.aka: Dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, push-down / let-down technique
card.note: Hump recurrence and technique-specific problems are discussed in the literature; evidence is largely retrospective.

quick.overview:
Preservation rhinoplasty is an approach in which the surgeon keeps the nose's original bony and cartilaginous bridge and lowers it as a unit, instead of the traditional method of cutting off a dorsal hump. The term was coined by Daniel in 2018, according to a case-series paper.

Surgical authors describe it as a shift in philosophy, with claims of better aesthetic and functional results that are still being tested.
quick.mechanism: The osseocartilaginous vault is mobilised as a single unit and pushed down or let down (push-down and let-down techniques), preserving natural dorsal lines and mucosa. Several classification systems and hybrid approaches have been proposed.
quick.risks: Reported problems include hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery. Evidence in the sources reviewed comprises retrospective series, a radiological comparison with hump resection, and registered trials.

lead: Preservation rhinoplasty, also called dorsal preservation rhinoplasty, refers to techniques that address a dorsal hump or the nasal profile by repositioning rather than removing the natural dorsum. A 2020 review notes a rekindled interest in dorsal preservation as an alternative to conventional hump resection, with claims of superior functional and aesthetic results, and describes mobilising the osseocartilaginous vault as a single unit to avoid disrupting natural structure.[1]

A 2018 article titled as a rhinoplasty revolution popularised the term, and a 2020 case series states that the term was coined by Daniel in 2018 and represents a fundamental change in philosophy.[2][3] Later papers proposed classification systems, hybrid structural approaches and guidelines.[4][5][6]
The evidence base consists of retrospective series and comparisons; no large randomised trial is present in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Push-down, let-down, cartilage conversion, hybrid osteoplasty

paras: Push-down and let-down are two main variants; one study used push-down for humps under 4 mm and let-down for larger ones.[7] A practical classification system, guidelines for primary rhinoplasty and a structural hybrid approach have been published, as have techniques converting cartilage to expand indications.[4][5][6][8][9]

A 100-case series with one-year follow-up reported on decision making in preservation rhinoplasty.[3] A study of 520 patients discussed reasons for dorsal hump recurrence after let-down or push-down surgery and proposed solutions.[7] A radiological study compared the effect on the internal nasal valve of dorsal preservation versus hump resection.[10] A review of current trends summarises the field.[11]

Human data are retrospective: a 153-patient primary series (100 with one-year follow-up), a 520-patient series on hump relapse, and a quantitative radiological comparison with hump resection.[3][7][10] Registered trials include a completed study of nasal valve angle and area (100 patients) and an active trial of hybrid osteoplasty versus osteotomy (200 patients).[12][13]

timeline.event: Term preservation rhinoplasty coined and article on a rhinoplasty revolution published.[2][3]
Review and modification of dorsal preservation techniques; 100-case series reported.[1][3]
Practical classification system and guidelines for dorsum preservation published.[4][5]
